mcqs.question: What stays constant across every grouping problem's implementation, regardless of what the signature computes?
options: It computes a different signature for every function call, invalidating past results
It requires items to already be sorted before grouping can begin
It stores only a count for each signature, discarding the original items
It appends each item to the list keyed by its computed signature, creating that list on first use — the loop body never changes, only the signature function does
mcqs.explanation: The group-by loop is identical across every variant — compute a key, append to that key's list — so the actual design work is choosing the signature, not the loop. Grouping preserves the original items rather than discarding them, and needs no prior sorting.

mcqs.question: What's the trade-off of using a 26-count-tuple key instead of a sorted-string key for grouping lowercase-English anagrams?
options: It reduces per-string cost from O(m log m) to O(m), but only remains correct if the alphabet is fixed and known in advance
It works correctly for any alphabet with no assumptions about its size
It has the exact same asymptotic cost as sorting, just implemented differently
It requires representing counts as floating-point numbers, introducing precision issues
mcqs.explanation: Counting is linear in string length while sorting pays a log factor, so the tuple key is asymptotically better — but a fixed-size tuple only makes sense when the alphabet itself has a fixed, known size, unlike the sorted string which needs no such assumption.

mcqs.question: Why can't you group overlapping intervals using the same canonical-key technique used for anagrams or digit sums?
options: A raw floating-point value is always safe to use as a grouping signature
Overlap-based grouping reduces to the exact same canonical-key technique as anagrams
Any two items that seem "similar" can always be grouped with a canonical key
A canonical key requires the grouping relation to be a true equivalence — reflexive, symmetric, and transitive — and interval overlap isn't transitive, so it needs sorting-and-merging instead
mcqs.explanation: A interval overlapping two others doesn't mean those two overlap each other, which breaks transitivity — the requirement a canonical-key signature depends on. Overlap-based grouping needs a different technique entirely, and raw floats are a known precision hazard as signatures.

mcqs.question: Your canonical signature is naturally a list of counts, but a list can't be used as a map key. What's the standard fix?
options: Convert the mutable structure to an immutable, hashable equivalent — a list of counts becomes a tuple, a set becomes a frozenset — before using it as a key
Use the mutable object directly; hashmaps hash objects by their memory identity, not their contents
Only string signatures are ever valid as map keys in any language
Wrap the mutable list in another list to make it hashable
mcqs.explanation: Converting to an immutable equivalent like a tuple gives a stable, hashable value that safely represents the same information. Wrapping in another list doesn't fix hashability, and hashmaps generally hash by value/content for these key types, not raw identity.

mcqs.question: What's the fastest way to tell whether a hashmap problem wants grouping or counting while reading the prompt?
options: Whether the input is a list of strings or a list of integers
Whether the expected output needs the original items back (grouping) or just a number or single representative value (counting)
Whether the map's keys happen to be strings or tuples
Whether the problem statement mentions a hashmap by name
mcqs.explanation: Grouping preserves and returns the original items bucketed together; counting discards them and returns only a count, max, or similar summary value — that's the distinguishing signal, independent of input type or key representation.
